discuss and make a class presentation on how households can adopt conservation of forage in coping with drought.

Critical thinking and Problem-solving: evaluation and decision-making skills as learners analyse and apply methods of conserving hay to cope with drought.
Communication and collaboration: speaking and dialogue skills as learners discuss ways of conserving forage to cope with drought in the context of rearing animals.
sub_strands.values: Peace: respect for diversity of opinions as learners discuss methods of conserving hay to cope with drought.
sub_strands.pcis: Disaster risk reduction as learners analyse and adopt applicable methods of conserving hay to cope with drought.

skills.name: Describe the methods of conserving forage to cope with drought
skills.mastery: Describes the methods of conserving forage to cope with drought (haymaking by baling or stacking, standing forage left uncut, keeping crop residues such as maize stover) and says why conserved feed keeps animals alive in a drought, and gives the reason in a new situation; in the app the child picks the right answer in new situations. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Feeding animals every day (Grade 8) is why feed must be kept for dry months. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
Drying to preserve (Grade 6) is the idea behind hay. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.name: Say how hay is made, baled or stacked and stored
skills.mastery: Says how hay is made: cut grass at flowering, dry it in the sun and turn it until it is dry but still green, bale it in a box baler or stack it on a raised base with a sloping top, cover it from rain, store it dry and off the ground, and feed it in the dry season; in the app the child picks the right step, order, material, reason or method in new situations. The practical (conserving forage by stacking or box-baling) is marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric indicator; the app asks only the knowledge half. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: The child knows the methods before making hay. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
Sun-drying steps (Grade 6) are used again for grass. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.assessed_by: teacher marks the practical with the KICD rubric

misconceptions.error: Thinks feed is conserved during the drought, when grass is short.

example.question: When should forage be conserved for a drought?
example.correct_answer: In the rainy season when there is plenty of grass

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks of acting when the problem is seen.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "During the drought" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a calendar: grass is plenty in April and gone in September.
misconceptions.feedback: Conserve forage when grass is plenty, in the rains, to feed animals in the drought.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks standing forage means grass cut and stood in heaps.

example.question: What is standing forage?
example.wrong_answer: Grass cut and stood in heaps
example.correct_answer: Grass left uncut in a fenced paddock to be grazed in the dry season

misconceptions.cause: The child pictures "standing" as stacked.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Grass cut and stood in heaps" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a fenced paddock left ungrazed in the rains.
misconceptions.feedback: Standing forage is grass left growing in a closed paddock for the dry season.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Burns maize stover after harvest instead of keeping it as feed.

example.question: What can be done with maize stover after harvest to help in a drought?
example.wrong_answer: Burn it to clear the shamba
example.correct_answer: Store it dry as animal feed

misconceptions.cause: Burning is the usual way to clear fields.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Burn it to clear the shamba" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what cattle eat when the grass is gone.
misconceptions.feedback: Keep maize stover dry as feed for the dry season.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks animals can always be moved to find grass, so there is no need to conserve feed.

example.question: Why is conserving feed better than moving animals in a drought?
example.correct_answer: Moving is far, costly and risky; stored feed keeps animals strong at home

misconceptions.cause: The child has heard of herders moving with animals.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Moving is always better" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Discuss the losses of animals in the last drought.
misconceptions.feedback: Stored feed keeps animals alive and strong at home in a drought.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Cuts grass for hay when it is old, dry and brown.

example.question: When is grass best cut for hay?
example.wrong_answer: When it is old, dry and brown
example.correct_answer: At flowering, when it is still green and leafy

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks dry grass is already hay.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "When it is old, dry and brown" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare green leafy grass and old brown stems: which would a cow choose?
misconceptions.feedback: Cut grass at flowering. Old brown grass has little feed value.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves bales out in the open after making them.

example.question: Where are hay bales kept after baling?
example.correct_answer: Under a roof or cover, off the ground

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks dry hay stays dry.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Out in the field" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a bale left out in rain: black and mouldy inside.
misconceptions.feedback: Store bales under cover and off the ground so rain and damp do not spoil them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Bales or stacks the grass while it is still wet.

example.question: What happens if hay is baled while still damp?
example.correct_answer: It goes mouldy and can heat up

misconceptions.cause: The child wants to finish quickly.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It keeps better" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Smell a damp bale left for a week.
misconceptions.feedback: Dry hay well before baling. Damp hay goes mouldy.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Stacks hay straight on the ground with a flat top.

example.question: How should a hay stack be built?
example.wrong_answer: On the ground with a flat top
example.correct_answer: On a raised base with a sloping, covered top

misconceptions.cause: The child does not think about damp from below and rain from above.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "On the ground with a flat top" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Pour water on a flat-topped and a sloping model stack.
misconceptions.feedback: Raise the stack and slope its top so rain runs off and the bottom stays dry.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

prepare leftover food for consumption through methods such as reheating or preparing another recipe to avoid wastage.
make presentations on various recipes adopted from leftover food to avoid food wastage.

sub_strands.core_competences: Creativity and Imagination: experimenting skills as learners explore different ways of preparing leftover food.
sub_strands.values: Integrity: utilising resources prudently to avoid wastage of resources in the preparation of leftover food.
sub_strands.pcis: Hygiene in handling of foods to prevent contamination and spoilage.
sub_strands.links: Learners relate the conservation of leftover foods to the spread of food-related diseases and illnesses learnt through Integrated Science.

outcomes.text: explain the importance of conserving leftover food at home
prepare leftover food to avoid wastage
embrace the use of leftover food to avoid food wastage

skills.name: Explain why leftover food should be conserved and kept safe
skills.mastery: Explains why leftover food is conserved at home (saves money and food, less waste) and how it is kept safe (cooled quickly, covered, kept cool and used within a day), and says unsafe leftovers cause food poisoning, and gives the reason in a new situation; in the app the child picks the right answer in new situations. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Keeping food cool and covered so germs do not grow came in Grade 8. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
What makes mould grow on food (Science Grade 6) is why leftovers spoil. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.name: Say how leftover food is reheated safely or made into a new dish
skills.mastery: Says how leftover food is prepared: check it smells and looks fine, reheat it once until steaming hot all through, or turn it into a new dish (fried rice, fried ugali, mukimo, soup), serve at once, and throw away food left out too long or reheated before; in the app the child picks the right step, order, material, reason or method in new situations. The practical (preparing leftover food to avoid wastage) is marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric indicator; the app asks only the knowledge half. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: The child knows how leftovers are kept safe before reheating them. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
Planning and cooking a meal (Grade 8) is used to make a new dish. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.assessed_by: teacher marks the practical with the KICD rubric

misconceptions.error: Leaves leftover food uncovered in the warm pot overnight.

example.question: How should leftover food be kept overnight?
example.correct_answer: Cooled quickly, covered and kept in a cool place

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks cooked food is safe whatever happens.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "In the warm pot, uncovered" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what flies and warmth do to food overnight.
misconceptions.feedback: Cool leftovers quickly, cover them and keep them cool.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks food that smells fine is always safe.

example.question: Leftover rice has been out all day in the heat but smells fine. Is it safe?
example.correct_answer: No, germs may have grown without changing the smell

misconceptions.cause: The child trusts the nose.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, it smells fine" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Explain some food-poisoning germs give no smell.
misconceptions.feedback: Food left out in the heat can be unsafe even if it smells fine.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks leftovers are rubbish to be thrown away.

example.question: Why conserve leftover food?
example.correct_answer: It saves food and money and cuts waste

misconceptions.cause: The child sees leftovers as scraps.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "There is no reason" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Add up the cost of food thrown away in a week.
misconceptions.feedback: Leftovers kept safely save food and money.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Keeps leftovers for many days without a fridge.

example.question: How long can leftovers be kept without a fridge?
example.correct_answer: Until the next meal or next day only

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks cooked food lasts like dry food.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A week" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show mould on githeri kept for three days.
misconceptions.feedback: Without a fridge, use leftovers by the next meal or next day.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Warms leftovers only until lukewarm.

example.question: How hot should reheated leftovers be?
example.correct_answer: Steaming hot all the way through

misconceptions.cause: The child heats until it is nice to eat.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Just warm" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Explain heat must reach the middle to kill germs.
misconceptions.feedback: Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot all through.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Mixes old leftovers with freshly cooked food to use them up.

example.question: Should yesterday's leftovers be stirred into today's fresh stew?
example.correct_answer: No, keep them apart and use the leftovers first, reheated once

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks mixing hides the old food safely.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, it saves food" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Explain germs in the old food spread through the whole pot.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not mix old leftovers into fresh food. Reheat and eat them on their own first.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Reheats the same leftovers again and again.

example.question: How many times should leftovers be reheated?
example.correct_answer: Once only

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks heating always makes food safe.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "As many times as needed" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Explain each cooling and warming lets germs grow again.
misconceptions.feedback: Reheat leftovers once only. Throw away what is left after that.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks leftovers can only be reheated, never made into something new.

example.question: What new dish can be made from leftover rice?
example.correct_answer: Fried rice or rice pudding

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen leftovers only warmed up.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "None, only reheating" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Make fried rice with leftover rice and vegetables.
misconceptions.feedback: Leftovers can become new dishes, like fried rice or mukimo.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: take an excursion or search for information on integrated farming practises to find out how components of integrated farming help in conserving resources.

design or sketch and make a model to illustrate integrated farming components such as fish rearing, rabbit keeping, poultry keeping and vegetable production on the same plot of land to show their relational benefits.
make class presentations on the models of integrated farming and the importance of integration in conserving resources.
key_inquiry_questions: How can integrated farming conserve resources?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and Imagination: observation and making connection skills as learners seek information, design and make a model to depict an integrated farming enterprise.
Critical thinking and Problem-solving: evaluation and decision-making skills as learners analyse the environment for components of integrated farming and design models of an integrated farming enterprise.
sub_strands.values:
Unity: teamwork as learners harness gifts and special skills of the group members in designing and making an integrated farming model.
Respect: accommodating diverse opinions while learners discuss and design a model of integrated farming.
sub_strands.pcis: Environmental awareness and protection as learners re-use locally available resources such as waste pieces of wood, cartons, cardboard and papers to design and make a model of integrated farming enterprise.
sub_strands.links: Learners apply skills of designing and choice of materials learnt in Pre-Technical Studies in the construction of an integrated farming model.

outcomes.text: describe components of integrated farming in conserving resources
make a model of integrated farming for the conservation of resources
appreciate the importance of integrated farming in the conservation of resources

skills.name: Describe the components of integrated farming and how each conserves resources
skills.mastery: Describes the components of integrated farming (fish rearing, rabbit keeping, poultry, vegetables, fruit trees, compost) on one plot and how each one's waste becomes another's input, conserving land, water, feed and money, and gives the reason in a new situation; in the app the child picks the right answer in new situations. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: The kitchen garden (Grade 8) is one component of integrated farming. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
Links between living things (Integrated Science Grade 9) are the idea behind integration. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.name: Say how an integrated farming model is designed to show the links between its parts
skills.mastery: Says how an integrated farming model is designed: sketch the plot, place each component where it can feed the next (rabbit hutch over the fish pond, poultry near the vegetables, compost near the garden), show the links with arrows (droppings to pond and garden, pond water to crops, crop waste to animals), choose materials and build it; in the app the child picks the right step, order, material, reason or method in new situations. The practical (making a model of integrated farming) is marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric indicator; the app asks only the knowledge half. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: The child knows the components before arranging them in a model. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
The model starts from a free-hand sketch (Pre-Technical Grade 7). Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.assessed_by: teacher marks the practical with the KICD rubric

misconceptions.error: Thinks integrated farming is any farm that keeps several things with no links between them.

example.question: What makes a farm "integrated"?
example.wrong_answer: Keeping many things, each on its own
example.correct_answer: The parts feed each other: one part's waste is another's input

misconceptions.cause: The child takes "integrated" to mean "many".
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Keeping many things, each on its own" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw arrows between the parts of a farm; a farm with no arrows is not integrated.
misconceptions.feedback: Integrated farming links the parts so the waste of one feeds another.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks animal droppings are waste with no use on the farm.

example.question: How can rabbit droppings be used in integrated farming?
example.correct_answer: To feed fish in the pond or manure the vegetables

misconceptions.cause: The child sees droppings as dirt.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "They are waste" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a hutch built over a fish pond.
misconceptions.feedback: Rabbit and poultry droppings manure crops or feed the fish pond.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks fish pond water is useless for crops.

example.question: How can water from a fish pond help the garden?
example.correct_answer: It is rich in nutrients and waters the vegetables

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks pond water is dirty.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It cannot" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Water two beds, one with pond water, and compare.
misconceptions.feedback: Fish pond water is full of nutrients. Use it to water crops.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks integrated farming needs more land than one enterprise.

example.question: Why does integrated farming suit a small plot?
example.wrong_answer: It does not; it needs more land
example.correct_answer: The parts share space and inputs, so a small plot gives more

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks more activities need more land.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It does not; it needs more land" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a small plot plan with a pond, hutch, poultry and beds.
misconceptions.feedback: Integrated farming uses a small plot well because the parts share space and inputs.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Draws arrows the wrong way, such as from the fish pond to the rabbits.

example.question: In a model, which way does the arrow go between the rabbit hutch and the fish pond?
example.wrong_answer: From the pond to the hutch
example.correct_answer: From the hutch to the pond (droppings feed the fish)

misconceptions.cause: The child draws arrows without asking what moves.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "From the pond to the hutch" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask what moves from one to the other.
misconceptions.feedback: Arrows show what moves: rabbit droppings go from the hutch to the pond.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Builds the model with no labels or key.

example.question: Why label the parts of an integrated farming model?
example.correct_answer: So others can see each component and the links between them

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks the model explains itself.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is not needed" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask a visitor to explain an unlabelled model.
misconceptions.feedback: Label each part and the arrows so the model shows how the farm works.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Places the compost pit far from the garden in the model.

example.question: Where is the compost pit best placed in an integrated plot?
example.correct_answer: Near the garden and the animal houses

misconceptions.cause: The child does not think about carrying work.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Far from the garden" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Count the steps to carry compost across the plot model.
misconceptions.feedback: Place the compost pit near the animals and the garden to save work.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Builds the model without a sketch, so parts do not fit.

example.question: What is done before building the model?
example.correct_answer: Sketch the plot and plan where each part goes

misconceptions.cause: The child is keen to build.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Start building at once" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a model where the pond covers the garden.
misconceptions.feedback: Sketch and plan the plot before you build.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

grow a selected short-season crop such as a vegetable, legume, or spice crop using organic gardening practises such as the use of organic manure, organic pesticides, mechanical weed control, use of organic foliar feed made from animal wastes and plants like Mexican sunflower.
share experiences through class presentations to appreciate the importance of organic gardening in the production of healthy foods.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should we practise organic gardening?
How can we produce food crops through organic gardening?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Learning to Learn: working collaboratively and organising own learning skills as learners grow crops using organic gardening practises.
Self-efficacy: planning skills as learners grow crops using organic farming practises.
sub_strands.values:
Unity: working in teams as learners undertake the project on growing crops using organic gardening practises.
Integrity: honesty as learners practise organic gardening practises.
sub_strands.pcis: Food health and safety as learners acquire skills of growing foods without use of agro-chemicals.
sub_strands.links: Learners relate organic gardening practises to farming practises in Social Studies.

outcomes.text: explain organic gardening practises in crop production
grow a crop using organic gardening practises
appreciate the importance of organic gardening in the production of healthy foods

skills.name: Explain organic gardening practices in crop production
skills.mastery: Explains organic gardening practices (organic manure and compost, organic pesticides, mechanical weed control, foliar feeds from animal waste and plants such as Mexican sunflower, crop rotation, mulching) and how they give healthy food without synthetic chemicals, and gives the reason in a new situation; in the app the child picks the right answer in new situations. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Controlling pests without harmful chemicals (Grade 8) is an organic practice. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
Using plant remains to improve soil (Grade 5) is at the heart of organic gardening. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.name: Say how organic inputs are prepared and used on a crop
skills.mastery: Says how organic inputs are prepared and used: compost made and dug in, a foliar feed made by soaking chopped Mexican sunflower or manure in water for two weeks and diluting it, an organic spray of chilli, garlic, ash or neem, applied early in the morning or evening, and weeds removed by hand or jembe; in the app the child picks the right step, order, material, reason or method in new situations. The practical (growing a crop using organic gardening practices) is marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric indicator; the app asks only the knowledge half. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: The child knows the practices before preparing the inputs. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.
Compost making (Grade 4) is the first organic input. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher.

skills.assessed_by: teacher marks the practical with the KICD rubric

misconceptions.error: Thinks organic gardening means doing nothing: no manure, no pest control.

example.question: What does organic gardening mean?
example.wrong_answer: Growing with no inputs or care at all
example.correct_answer: Growing with natural inputs such as compost and organic sprays, not synthetic chemicals

misconceptions.cause: The child hears "natural" as "left alone".
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Growing with no inputs or care at all" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare an organic bed (compost, care) with an untended one.
misconceptions.feedback: Organic gardening uses natural inputs and care, not synthetic chemicals.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks organic crops cannot grow well at all.

example.question: Can an organic garden give a good harvest?
example.correct_answer: Yes, with good compost, foliar feeds and care

misconceptions.cause: The child has heard that chemicals are needed for big harvests.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, never" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show the class organic bed at harvest.
misconceptions.feedback: Well-fed organic soil gives good harvests of healthy food.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks food grown with chemicals and organic food are no different for health or soil.

example.question: Why do people choose organic food?
example.correct_answer: No harmful chemical residues, and the soil and water stay healthy

misconceptions.cause: The child cannot see residues and assumes none.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "There is no difference" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Read a pesticide label's waiting period before harvest.
misconceptions.feedback: Organic food has no synthetic chemical residues and keeps soil and water healthy.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks crop rotation is not part of organic gardening.

example.question: Why is crop rotation used in organic gardening?

misconceptions.error: Puts the dryer in the shade so the vegetables do not burn.

example.question: Where is a sun dryer placed?
example.correct_answer: In full sun, facing the sun, raised and tilted

misconceptions.cause: The child fears the sun will cook the food.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "In the shade" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Measure how long drying takes in shade and in sun.
misconceptions.feedback: Place the dryer in full sun, facing the sun.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Never cleans the trays between batches.

example.question: Why clean the dryer trays after each batch?
example.correct_answer: Old bits grow mould and attract pests that spoil the next batch

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks dry trays stay clean.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "There is no need" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show mould on a tray left with old bits.
misconceptions.feedback: Clean the trays after each batch.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves the dried vegetables in the dryer for days after they are crisp.

example.question: What is done once the vegetables are crisp?
example.correct_answer: Cool and store them in a sealed, dry container

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks the dryer is a store.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Leave them in the dryer" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show crisp vegetables gone limp after a night in the dryer.
misconceptions.feedback: Take out crisp vegetables, cool them and seal them in a dry container.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Agriculture teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.
